title: India Attracts Nearly $10 Billion in NRI Deposits as RBI's Special Programme Offers Up to 7% Dollar Returns

body:
Key Takeaways
  • India's RBI program attracted nearly $10 billion in NRI deposits.
  • NRI deposit rates increased to 7% due to RBI's new scheme.
  • The program is tax-exempt for eligible NRI and OCI depositors.
  • Economists predict total inflows could reach $30-$60 billion.
  • The rupee faces pressure, currently near its all-time low.

India has attracted roughly $10 billion in inflows through the Reserve Bank of India's special deposit programme for overseas Indians, according to Reuters, as the central bank works to shore up foreign exchange reserves and stabilize the rupee.

How the Programme Works

The RBI announced a zero-cost foreign exchange swap facility at its June 5 policy meeting, effectively allowing banks to offer significantly higher returns on Foreign Currency Non-Resident (FCNR-B) deposits. Under normal conditions, banks bear a hedging cost of 2 to 3 percent when raising dollar deposits, which caps the interest rates they can offer. The RBI's new scheme absorbs that currency mismatch on its own balance sheet, letting banks pass the savings on to depositors. The result: NRI deposit rates have jumped from the usual 3.5 to 5 percent range to as high as 7 percent on dollar deposits. Major banks have moved quickly — HDFC Bank raised rates by 235 to 265 basis points to 6 percent on three- to five-year deposits, State Bank of India hiked by up to 300 basis points, and AU Small Finance Bank and Yes Bank are offering rates between 7 and 7.1 percent.

Why This Matters for NRIs

For the estimated 32 million overseas Indians worldwide, the programme offers a rare combination: high dollar-denominated returns with no currency risk, since both principal and interest are repaid in the deposited currency. The deposits are exempt from Indian taxation for eligible NRI and OCI depositors, and the window runs until September 30, 2026, with a minimum tenor of three years and a one-year lock-in period. A June 23 clarification further sweetened the deal by allowing banks to lend against these deposits and offer leverage, making the programme more attractive for larger depositors.

The Bigger Picture

The $10 billion raised so far represents only a fraction of the total anticipated inflows. Economists and bankers estimate the programme could attract between $30 billion and $60 billion in foreign currency deposits — critical support for the rupee, which has been under pressure from surging oil prices.
Impact on the Rupee and Future Projections
›Projected inflows could reach $30-$60 billion.
›Rupee weakened past 96 per US dollar.
›Near all-time low of 96.96 per dollar.
›Rising oil prices add pressure on external finances.
The rupee, which had rallied to nearly 94 per US dollar after the RBI's initial measures, has since weakened past 96, sitting less than 1 percent from its all-time low of 96.96 per dollar. Rising hostilities between the US and Iran have pushed Brent crude over 20 percent above recent lows, adding to pressure on India's external finances. For NRIs considering the scheme, the key decision point is clear: the September 30 deadline means the window to lock in these elevated rates is narrowing.
